Chapter 5 Exploratory Data Analysis 5.1 Exploratory vs. Confirmatory Research 5.2 Pre-registering Confirmatory Research 5.3 Doing both Exploratory and Confirmatory Research

Chapter 5 Exploratory Data Analysis 5.1 Exploratory vs. Confirmatory Research Before we discuss how to conduct the statistical tests you are familiar with, it is first important for us to understand why you would choose to conduct a statistical test and what is the right parameters to do so. Chris Chambers in his 2019 book ‘The seven deadly sins of psychology: A manifesto for reforming the culture of scientific practice’ emphasises the difference between hypothesis-generating (exploratory) and hypothesis-confirming (confirmatory) analysis. When deriving your research question and aims, you should be clear about whether it is exploratory or confirmatory. An exploratory research question would look like How are different patterns of social media use associated with different aspects of adolescent well-being? A confirmatory research question would like like Do adolescents who use social media for more than three hours per day report lower sleep quality than adolescents who use it for less than one hour per day? This confirmatory research question would naturally lead on to specific hypotheses, for example, Adolescents who use social media for more than three hours per day will report lower sleep quality than adolescents who use it for less than one hour per day. Importantly, confirmatory research with hypotheses requires a power analysis to determine whether you are able to detect an effect, should it exist. Exploratory research does not require this. 5.2 Pre-registering Confirmatory Research If you have confirmatory research questions with prior hypothesis, you should be completing a pre-registration prior to conducting your analyses. If you do not do this, there is a danger of HARKing (Hypothesising After Results are Known) (Kerr, 1998), where scientists alter their original hypothesis in their published write-up to better fit with the patterns they have observed in the data. There is also the danger of p-hacking, where unplanned analyses are carried out until one analysis manages to find a p-value that is smaller than .05. You can pre-register your study on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/). Even better, you could submit the introduction and methods of your paper as a Registered Report format to a journal who provide you with peer-review before you carry out your analysis and guarantee they will publish the results and discussion no matter what you find. A list of journals that support the registered report format can be found here: https://www.cos.io/initiatives/registered-reports. Pre-registration also reduces the chances of something going unpublished solely because it has null results and interestingly since the registered report format has been increasingly used, it has been found that only 44% of results in registered reports are ‘positive’, compared to 96% of results in traditional psychology publications (Scheel et al., 2021) 5.3 Doing both Exploratory and Confirmatory Research The good news is you do not need to choose between confirmatory and exploratory research. You may have a few hypotheses based on prior literature on which you design your study. Following your study, you may choose to conduct further exploratory research on your results based on patterns you have observed. The most important thing is to be clear about which research questions were designed before and after seeing the data.

Chapter 6 Significance 6.1 Statistical significance 6.2 Clinical significance and effect sizes

Chapter 6 Significance There are two types of significance: statistical significance and clinical significance. Consider a research trial finds a statistically significant difference between participants’ depression scores before and after 12 sessions of therapy which amounts to a 1.0 change on the PHQ-9. Despite this statistically significant chaange, it’s unlikely that those participants would feel that this therapy had a meaningful impact on their lives, despite reaching statistical significance. Statistical significance: Is this effect real or due to random variation? Clinical significance: Is this effect large enough to matter? 6.1 Statistical significance Statistics is often done using the frequentist (or classical) approach which is based in null hypothesis statistical testing (NHST). This type of statistics always starts with a null hypothesis (H₀) which usually states that there is no difference between groups, conditions or variables and an alternative hypothesis that an effect or difference exists (Ha). After data are collected, a test statistic is calculated. The specific test statistic depends on the analysis being conducted (e.g., t for t-tests, F for ANOVAs, and χ² for chi-square tests). These statistics represent the size of the observed effect relative to the amount of random variation expected under the null hypothesis. In other words, they indicate how far the observed data deviate from what we would expect if there were truly no effect. The test statistic is then compared against its sampling distribution, which allows a p-value to be calculated. The p-value represents the probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as those observed, assuming that the null hypothesis is true. Therefore, a smaller p-value indicates that the observed data would be relatively unlikely if there were no real effect. For example, a p-value of 0.03 means that, if the null hypothesis were true, there would be a 3% probability of obtaining results this extreme or more extreme due to random variation. In 1925, Fisher published Statistical Methods for Research Workers and suggested that results occurring less than 5% of the time under the null hypothesis should be considered noteworthy. Over time, this suggestion became formalised into the convention of using p < .05 as a threshold for rejecting the null hypothesis, although Fisher himself did not intend this to be a rigid rule. An alternative approach to frequentist/classical statistics is Bayesian statistics. A key limitation of NHST is that it does not allow researchers to directly calculate the probability that a hypothesis is true. Instead, it evaluates how compatible the observed data are with the null hypothesis. Bayesian statistics takes a different approach by estimating the relative evidence for competing hypotheses (such as the null and alternative hypotheses) and allows researchers to update their beliefs about hypotheses in light of new data. Question 1 What is the purpose of the null hypothesis (H₀) in frequentist statistics? – Select an answer – It usually states that there is no difference or effect It states that the researcher’s theory is definitely true It calculates the size of the effect being studied It proves that groups are identical Check answer Question 2 What does a test statistic represent? – Select an answer – The probability that the alternative hypothesis is true The size of the observed effect relative to expected random variation The number of participants needed for a study The percentage of participants who improved Check answer Question 3 A study reports p = 0.025. What does this mean? – Select an answer – There is a 3% chance that the alternative hypothesis is true If the null hypothesis were true, there would be a 2.5% chance of observing results this extreme or more extreme The study has a 97.5% chance of being correct The effect size is 2.5% Check answer 6.2 Clinical significance and effect sizes Clinical significance tells us whether our finding is large enough to be meaningful in pratice. There are several ways of assessing clinical significance. Three common approaches are: 1. Reporting an effect size: this tells us how large the observed difference or association is, rather than simply whether it is statistically significant. 2. Comparing the effect with a pre-established minimally clinically important difference (MCID): this tells us whether the change is large enough to be considered meaningful from a clinical perspective. 3. Reporting the proportion of participants who achieve a clinically meaningful improvement: for example, the percentage of patients whose symptoms improve by at least a pre-defined amount. 6.2.1 Effect sizes An effect size is a measure of the magnitude of a finding. The appropriate effect sizes depends on the type of analysis being conducted. For example: Differences between groups: mean difference or standardardised mean difference like Cohen’s d Associations between variables: correlation coefficient (r) Categorical outcomes: odds ratios or risk ratios Once you have calculated an effect size, there are then common conventions to interpreting the effect size: Effect size Small Medium Large Cohen’s d 0.20 0.50 0.80 r 0.10 0.30 0.50 Odds ratio 1.68 3.47 6.71 Risk ratio 1.22 1.86 3.00 Chen, H., Cohen, P., & Chen, S. (2010). How big is a big odds ratio? Interpreting the magnitudes of odds ratios in epidemiological studies. Communications in Statistics—simulation and Computation®, 39(4), 860-864. Sullivan, G. M., & Feinn, R. (2012). Using effect size—or why the P value is not enough. Journal of graduate medical education, 4(3), 279-282 6.2.2 Minimally clinically important differences (MCID) Another way of assessing clinical significance is by using pre-established thresholds of minimally clinically important differences on commonly used outcome measures. For example, the PHQ-9 has a MCID of 3.7 points (Bauer-Staeb et al., 2021) and the GAD-7 has a MCID of 4 points (Toussaint et al., 2020). When comparing participants before and after the study, you could report the average change in your primary outcome measure and compare this to the MCID and you could also calculate what percentage of individual participants’ scores changed more than the MCID. Bauer-Staeb, C., et al. (2021). Effective dose 50 method as the minimal clinically important difference: Evidence from depression trials. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology. Toussaint, A., et al. (2020). Sensitivity to change and minimal clinically important difference of the 7-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder Questionnaire (GAD-7). Journal of Affective Disorders. 6.2.3 Proportion of participants reaching clinically meaningful improvement Finally, you may choose to assess clinical significance by reporting what percentage of participants reached meaningful improvement. You can do this using MCID as noted above. If you are using an outcome measure with pre-established cut-offs, you may choose to report how many participants changed from having ‘moderate’ to ‘mild’ symptoms on the measure you have used. For example, the CORE-10 categorises psychological distress as 0-10 = healthy 11-15 = mild distress 16-20 = moderate distress 21-25 = moderately severe distress 26-40 = severe distress Then after an intervention using the CORE-10 as an outcome measure, you might want to report what proportion of individual participants decreased from severe to moderate distress or from moderate distress to healthy. Descriptives -> Sleep 7.3 Pre-analysis steps It is essential to examine your data before conducting your analyses. This helps you understand the distribution of variables, exmaning missing data and assess the assumptions relevant to the statistical analyses you plan to conduct. 7.3.1 Normality Normality of variables is an assumption for many analyses. Occasionally, data will be non-normal. Normality can be assessed in multiple ways: Descriptively, by looking at skewness and kurtosis Testing using Shapiro-Wilk. If the test is significant (p < .05), that indicates a departure from normality Visually by inspecting plots If you find some indications of a variable being non-normally distributed, it may not be an issue especially if there is a large sample size. If all assessments of normality indicate that the non-normality is severe and the sample size is not particularly large… 7.3.1.1 Transformation -positive skew, square-root, logarithmic -negative skew - options here? detail in JASP Check the data afterwards, how is the skew now? 7.3.1.2 Non-parametric tests In particularly small sample sizes where data skew is severe
